<!-- data-checksum: f354a6da47f62ead35825a3d2b8ef6d9 -->

PROMs are collected at several visits, and patients miss some of them. [Page 9](../catalog/09-three-plus-matched.qmd#repeated-measures-anova) analyzed repeated scores with repeated-measures ANOVA, which only uses patients measured at every visit. A **linear mixed model** uses every score from every patient, and answers the questions a PROM study usually asks: how much do patients improve, by when, and does recovery differ between groups?

The examples use KOOS JR, the knee score, in the 330 total knee replacements. Hips answer a different questionnaire (HOOS JR), and a point on one isn't guaranteed to equal a point on the other, so the two aren't mixed in one model. The last example, on whether recovery differs between groups, uses the EFAS score from the boot vs cast trial on [page 6](../catalog/06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#unpaired-t), which also has four visits.

::: {.callout-note}
## 💡 How this page works
Run the code blocks in order, from the top: later blocks use the packages, data and models made earlier.

Each knee is treated as its own patient until the section on [bilateral patients](#bilateral).
:::

## Why not repeated-measures ANOVA? {#why-mixed-models}

Count how many of the four visits each knee has a score for:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(lmerTest)        # lme4's lmer(), plus p-values for its fixed effects
library(emmeans)         # estimated marginal means
library(splines)         # natural cubic splines, for time as a curve

proms <- read_csv("data/proms_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

knees <- proms |>
  filter(instrument == "KOOS JR", !is.na(prom_score)) |>          # every knee score that exists
  mutate(visit = factor(visit, levels = c("preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr")))

knees |>
  count(case_id, name = "visits") |>            # scores per knee
  count(visits, name = "knees")                 # knees with 1, 2, 3 or 4 scores
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import patsy
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

proms = pd.read_csv("data/proms_long.csv")

knees = proms[(proms["instrument"] == "KOOS JR") & proms["prom_score"].notna()].copy()    # every knee score that exists
visits = ["preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr"]
knees["visit"] = pd.Categorical(knees["visit"], categories=visits)               # pre-op first: the reference

print(knees.groupby("case_id").size().value_counts().sort_index())   # knees with 1, 2, 3 or 4 scores
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
1      4
2     28
3    106
4    192
Name: count, dtype: int64
```


:::
:::

:::





All 330 knees have at least one score, 1146 scores in all, but only 192 knees have all four. Repeated-measures ANOVA would drop the other 138 knees (42%) together with every score they did give. A mixed model keeps all 1146 scores.

Dropping patients isn't only wasteful. It can bias the result, and that depends on why scores are missing:
- **Missing completely at random:** a missed visit has nothing to do with the patient's recovery (the clinic rescheduled, the patient moved). Both methods are unbiased; the mixed model is more precise because it uses more data.
- **Missing at random:** missing depends on things you measured, such as an earlier score. A patient who scored badly at 6 weeks is less likely to return at 3 months. Repeated-measures ANOVA is then biased, because the patients it keeps recovered better; a mixed model is still unbiased, as long as the model describes how a knee's scores are related, because it uses the earlier scores to fill the picture in.
- **Missing not at random:** missing depends on the score that wasn't collected (patients stay away *because* their knee is worse that week). Nothing fixes this from the data alone. Say so as a limitation.

## A random intercept for each knee {#random-intercept}

Scores from the same knee are related: a knee that starts low tends to stay lower than average. A mixed model handles this with a **random intercept**: each knee gets its own baseline level, shifted up or down from the average. The **fixed effects** (here, the visits) describe the average patient; the random intercepts describe how much knees differ from that average.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
knee_model <- lmer(prom_score ~ visit + (1 | case_id), data = knees)   # (1 | case_id): an intercept per knee
print(summary(knee_model), correlation = FALSE)
```

## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
knee_model = smf.mixedlm("prom_score ~ visit", knees, groups="case_id").fit(reml=True)   # groups: an intercept per knee
print(knee_model.summary())
```

:::

Reading the output:
- **Fixed effects:** the average KOOS JR was 50.0 before surgery (the intercept), and higher by 12.5 points at 6 weeks, 24.2 at 3 months and 33.9 at 1 year. Each visit's coefficient is its difference from pre-op.
- **Random effects:** knees' own baseline levels vary around the average with an SD of 8.8 points (R's "case_id (Intercept)" row; Python's "case_id Var" row gives the variance, 8.84² = 78.1). The scores also vary from visit to visit within a knee with a residual SD of 8.6 points.
- **How much of the variation is between knees:** 78.1 / (78.1 + 73.5) = 0.52, the intraclass correlation ([page 17](17-agreement.qmd#icc) uses the same idea for raters). About half of the spread in scores comes from knees differing from each other; that's why the scores can't be treated as independent.
- **REML:** both programs fit the model by restricted maximum likelihood, the standard choice for estimating it.

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: degrees of freedom
The estimates agree. The standard errors agree to three or four significant figures: lme4 computes them with the knee and residual variances held at their estimates, statsmodels from the curvature of the whole likelihood. The p-values and CIs differ a little more. lmerTest gives each fixed effect a t test with **Satterthwaite** degrees of freedom, an approximation to how much information the estimate rests on. statsmodels uses a z test, as if the degrees of freedom were infinite. With 330 knees the difference is in the third decimal place; with a small study, trust R's.
:::

## Estimated marginal means {#estimated-marginal-means}

Report the model's estimate at each visit, with its 95% CI. These are the **estimated marginal means** (EMMs): the average score the model expects at each visit, using every knee, including those with missed visits.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
knee_means <- emmeans(knee_model, ~ visit, lmer.df = "satterthwaite")
knee_means
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 visit emmean    SE  df lower.CL upper.CL
 preop   50.0 0.688 708     48.6     51.3
 6wk     62.5 0.704 745     61.2     63.9
 3mo     74.2 0.716 772     72.8     75.6
 1yr     83.9 0.733 811     82.5     85.3

Degrees-of-freedom method: satterthwaite 
Confidence level used: 0.95 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# the planned comparison: 1 year minus pre-op (one comparison, so no adjustment; page 15)
confint(contrast(knee_means, method = list("1yr - preop" = c(-1, 0, 0, 1))))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 contrast    estimate    SE  df lower.CL upper.CL
 1yr - preop     33.9 0.734 838     32.5     35.3

Degrees-of-freedom method: satterthwaite 
Confidence level used: 0.95 
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
def marginal_means(model, grid):
    """The model's average score for each row of grid (fixed effects only), with its standard error and 95% CI."""
    X = patsy.build_design_matrices([model.model.data.model_spec], grid, return_type="dataframe")[0]
    beta = model.fe_params
    cov = model.cov_params().loc[beta.index, beta.index]
    means = grid.copy()
    means["emmean"] = X @ beta
    means["se"] = np.sqrt(np.diag(X @ cov @ X.T))
    means["lower"] = means["emmean"] - 1.96 * means["se"]
    means["upper"] = means["emmean"] + 1.96 * means["se"]
    return means

visit_grid = pd.DataFrame({"visit": pd.Categorical(visits, categories=visits)})
knee_means = marginal_means(knee_model, visit_grid)
print(knee_means.round(2))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   visit  emmean    se  lower  upper
0  preop   49.99  0.69  48.65  51.34
1    6wk   62.53  0.70  61.15  63.92
2    3mo   74.21  0.72  72.81  75.62
3    1yr   83.89  0.73  82.46  85.33
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
# the planned comparison: 1 year minus pre-op
print(knee_model.fe_params["visit[T.1yr]"], knee_model.conf_int().loc["visit[T.1yr]"].to_list())
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
33.898828315446195 [32.461019988411564, 35.336636642480826]
```


:::
:::

:::





- **emmean, lower.CL / upper.CL:** KOOS JR averaged 50.0 (95% CI 48.6 to 51.3) before surgery, 62.5 at 6 weeks, 74.2 at 3 months and 83.9 (95% CI 82.5 to 85.3) at 1 year.
- **The contrast:** the planned comparison, the improvement from pre-op to 1 year: 33.9 points (95% CI 32.5 to 35.3). Choose such comparisons in advance; comparing every pair of visits would need an adjustment ([page 15](15-post-hoc.qmd#planned-comparisons)).

The 192 knees with all four scores average 49.2 before surgery and 84.0 at 1 year. That's close to the mixed model, as expected here: in this synthetic cohort, visits were missed almost entirely at random: by chance, or because follow-up had ended. With real patients you can't count on that, and the mixed model's answer, which uses all 330 knees, is the one to report.

## Time: categories or a curve? {#time}

So far each visit has its own mean: **time as categories**. That fits when everyone is seen at the same few scheduled visits, and it makes no assumption about the shape of recovery. The alternative is **time as a number**, days since surgery, with a curve. That suits many or irregular visits, but the curve's shape must be right. Recovery isn't a straight line, so use a natural cubic spline ([page 12](../catalog/12-predict-from-several.qmd#multiple-nonlinear-regression) explains splines):

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
curve_model <- lmer(prom_score ~ ns(visit_days, df = 3) + (1 | case_id), data = knees)

days <- tibble(visit_days = c(-14, 42, 90, 365))           # the scheduled visit days
on_days <- predict(curve_model, newdata = days, re.form = NA)   # re.form = NA: the average knee
on_days
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
       1        2        3        4 
50.10003 62.67787 73.98054 84.07408 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
curve <- tibble(visit_days = -27:395)
curve$prom_score <- predict(curve_model, newdata = curve, re.form = NA)
ggplot(curve, aes(visit_days, prom_score)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = summary(knee_means) |> mutate(visit_days = c(-14, 42, 90, 365)), aes(y = emmean)) +
  labs(x = "Days since surgery", y = "KOOS JR")
```

::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
day_knots = list(knees["visit_days"].quantile([1/3, 2/3]))     # the same knots R's ns(df = 3) uses
day_low, day_high = knees["visit_days"].min(), knees["visit_days"].max()
curve_model = smf.mixedlm("prom_score ~ cr(visit_days, knots=day_knots, lower_bound=day_low, upper_bound=day_high,"
                          " constraints='center')", knees, groups="case_id").fit(reml=True)

days = pd.DataFrame({"visit_days": [-14, 42, 90, 365]})        # the scheduled visit days
on_days = curve_model.predict(days)                            # the average knee
print(on_days.round(2))
```

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
ax.plot(curve["visit_days"], curve_model.predict(curve))
ax.scatter(days["visit_days"], knee_means["emmean"])

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](16-mixed-models_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png)

:::





The curve passes close to the visit means (the points): 62.7 at 6 weeks and 84.1 at 1 year, against 62.5 and 83.9. But look between 3 months and 1 year. No knee was scored there, and the curve invents a peak of about 89 points at around 8 months, then falls. With a few fixed visits, a curve has nothing to follow between them. Categories are simpler, make no such claims, and are what the rest of this page uses.

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: a straight line for time
`prom_score ~ visit_days` would force recovery to be a straight line: as steep between 3 months and 1 year as in the first 6 weeks. Always plot the visit means first. If you use time as a number, let it bend.
:::

## Does recovery differ between groups? {#group-by-time}

To ask whether recovery with a boot differs from recovery with a cast, add arm and its **interaction** with visit. The interaction lets each arm have its own pattern of change. Its test asks whether the patterns differ, which is the question; the main effect of arm alone only compares the average levels. The model uses all 431 EFAS scores from the 120 randomized patients, although only 80 have all four.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
trial <- read_csv("data/foot_ankle_rct_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(!is.na(efas)) |>
  mutate(visit = factor(visit, levels = c("6wk", "3mo", "6mo", "12mo")),
         arm = factor(arm, levels = c("cast", "boot")))

arm_model <- lmer(efas ~ visit * arm + (1 | patient_id), data = trial)
arm_anova <- anova(arm_model)                           # F tests, Satterthwaite degrees of freedom
arm_anova
```

## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests

trial = pd.read_csv("data/foot_ankle_rct_long.csv")
trial = trial[trial["efas"].notna()].copy()
trial_visits = ["6wk", "3mo", "6mo", "12mo"]
trial["visit"] = pd.Categorical(trial["visit"], categories=trial_visits)       # 6 weeks first: the reference
trial["arm"] = pd.Categorical(trial["arm"], categories=["cast", "boot"])        # cast first: the reference

arm_model = smf.mixedlm("efas ~ visit * arm", trial, groups="patient_id").fit(reml=True)

interaction = [name for name in arm_model.fe_params.index if ":" in name]     # the three visit x arm terms
arm_wald = arm_model.wald_test(" = 0, ".join(interaction) + " = 0", scalar=True)   # do the patterns differ?
print(arm_wald.statistic, arm_wald.pvalue)                                          # chi-square on 3 df, p-value
```

arm_grid["arm"] = pd.Categorical(arm_grid["arm"], categories=["cast", "boot"])

```{.python .cell-code}
def arm_difference(model, visit):
    """Boot minus cast at one visit: the estimate and its standard error, from the fixed effects."""
    two = pd.DataFrame({"visit": pd.Categorical([visit, visit], categories=trial_visits),
                        "arm": pd.Categorical(["boot", "cast"], categories=["cast", "boot"])})
    X = patsy.build_design_matrices([model.model.data.model_spec], two, return_type="dataframe")[0]
    L = (X.iloc[0] - X.iloc[1]).to_numpy()                # the contrast: boot's row minus cast's row
    beta = model.fe_params
    cov = model.cov_params().loc[beta.index, beta.index].to_numpy()
    return float(L @ beta.to_numpy()), float(np.sqrt(L @ cov @ L))

gaps = pd.DataFrame([(visit, *arm_difference(arm_model, visit)) for visit in trial_visits],
                    columns=["visit", "difference", "se"])
gaps["lower"] = gaps["difference"] - 1.96 * gaps["se"]
gaps["upper"] = gaps["difference"] + 1.96 * gaps["se"]
gaps["p"] = 2 * stats.norm.sf(np.abs(gaps["difference"] / gaps["se"]))
gaps["p_holm"] = multipletests(gaps["p"], method="holm")[1]       # Holm across all four visits
print(gaps.round(3))
```

:::





- **visit:arm, F = 25.73 on 3 and 310 df, p < 0.001:** the patterns differ. Python's Wald test gives the undivided statistic, 77.15 on 3 degrees of freedom, also p < 0.001.
- **The EMMs and the differences (boot minus cast)** show how. At 6 weeks the boot led by 3.0 points, and at 3 months the boot led by 3.6 points (17.34 vs 13.78). By 6 months the gap was 0.4 points, and at 12 months it was −0.4 points (95% CI −1.5 to 0.7): the gap had closed.

These numbers differ a little from [page 6](../catalog/06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#unpaired-t)'s, which used only the 3-month scores: there the 95% CI for the 3-month difference was 2.4 to 4.8, and here it's 2.5 to 4.6, mostly because the model assumes the same spread at all four visits (SD 2.9), and the 3-month scores spread a little wider (SD 3.2 within each arm). Two cautions. EFAS scores crowd toward their maximum by 12 months (24 points for 7 of 55 patients with a boot and 8 of 47 with a cast), so the model's means are approximate there. And the cast arm missed more 12-month visits (13 against 5): the model keeps those patients' earlier scores, which helps as long as the missed visits are [missing at random](#why-mixed-models).

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: read an interaction through its means
A clear interaction says the gap between the arms changes over time. It doesn't say the boot is better: it depends on when you look. At 12 months, Holm-adjusted p = 0.898 means the data can't show a difference; it doesn't show the arms are the same, and the CI still runs from 1.5 points in the cast's favor to 0.7 in the boot's. Report the EMMs and the difference with their CIs so readers can see both.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: the differences between arms
Python computes the differences from the fixed effects with z tests, so its Holm-adjusted p-values differ in the third decimal (0.897 against 0.898).
:::

## Bilateral patients {#bilateral}

46 of the knee patients had both knees replaced, so 92 of the 330 knees come in pairs. The two knees share the same person, so their scores may be related beyond what each knee's own intercept captures. The standard fix is a second random intercept, for the patient, with knees **nested** in patients: in lme4, `(1 | patient_id/case_id)`; in statsmodels, `groups="patient_id"` with a variance component for `case_id`.

In this cohort the patient-level intercept comes out at almost exactly zero (lme4 warns that the fit is "singular"), so the knee model above is enough. In your data, fit the nested model and report it unless it is singular. [Page 3](../foundations/03-distributions.qmd#paired) explains why bilateral patients need care, and [page 14](../survival/14-cox-regression.qmd#stratified-cox) shows the survival-analysis version.

## How to report it {#reporting}

> **Methods:** KOOS JR scores before surgery and at 6 weeks, 3 months and 1 year were analyzed with a linear mixed model, with visit as a categorical fixed effect and a random intercept for each knee, fitted by restricted maximum likelihood. All available scores were used, including those from knees that missed a visit. The planned comparison was the change from before surgery to 1 year. Estimated marginal means are reported with 95% CIs.
>
> **Results:** Of 330 knees, 192 (58.2%) had all four scores; all 1146 scores were analyzed. The estimated mean KOOS JR was 50.0 (95% CI 48.6 to 51.3) before surgery and 83.9 (95% CI 82.5 to 85.3) at 1 year; change 33.9 points (95% CI 32.5 to 35.3).

For the comparison between a boot and a cast:

> **Methods:** EFAS scores at 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months and 12 months were analyzed with a linear mixed model with visit, arm and their interaction as fixed effects and a random intercept for each patient, fitted by restricted maximum likelihood. All available scores were used. The interaction was tested with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. Differences between arms at each visit are reported with 95% CIs and Holm-adjusted p-values.
>
> **Results:** Of 120 randomized patients, 80 (66.7%) had all four scores; all 431 scores were analyzed. At 3 months the estimated mean EFAS score was 17.3 (95% CI 16.6 to 18.1) with a boot and 13.8 (95% CI 13.0 to 14.5) with a cast (difference 3.6 points, 95% CI 2.5 to 4.6; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). At 12 months it was 20.2 (95% CI 19.4 to 20.9) with a boot and 20.6 (95% CI 19.8 to 21.4) with a cast (difference −0.4 points, 95% CI −1.5 to 0.7; Holm-adjusted p = 0.898). For the visit × arm interaction, F(3, 310) = 25.73 (p < 0.001).
